Title: What did you hand over, and what did you take back?
Detail_lesson: Most of us have already moved some part of the work to an agent: a migration, a test file, a first pass at a bug, the commit message nobody reads. Some of it stuck. Some of it came back after the second or third time you spent longer correcting the output than you would have spent typing it. Name one task you genuinely stopped doing by hand, and one you tried to hand over and reclaimed. The reclaimed one is the more interesting half: it tells us where the current boundary actually sits, as opposed to where the demos say it sits.
CustomInstruction: Name the specific task, not the category. Say what happened the third time you tried it, not the first.

Title: If an agent can build it from the ticket, who writes the ticket?
Detail_lesson: When the distance from a written intent to a running branch collapses to minutes, the written intent becomes the expensive part. Three positions are all defensible. One: specs get more rigorous than they have ever been, because ambiguity now produces confident wrong code instead of a question in standup. Two: specs get cheaper and more disposable, because when three implementations cost an afternoon you stop arguing and go look. Three: the ticket stops existing and the branch becomes the proposal. Pick the one your team is actually drifting toward and say whether that drift is a good thing.
CustomInstruction: Two or three sentences. Say which way your team is drifting, not which way it should drift.

Title: The machine wrote it and the machine reviewed it. What are you reviewing?
Detail_lesson: A second agent will find the null dereference, the missing await, the off-by-one, and it will find them faster and more consistently than you will at 4pm on a Thursday. That leaves the human reviewer holding something else, and it is not obvious what. Candidates: the interface and who else now depends on it; the blast radius if this is wrong; whether the tests would fail if the code were wrong; whether this change should exist at all. Or the opposite answer, that human review of the diff stops entirely and moves to production behaviour. Say what you would actually spend your review attention on now, and what you would consciously let through unread.
CustomInstruction: Say what you would stop reading. An answer that keeps reviewing everything is not an answer.

Title: The agent wrote the code and the tests. What are the tests worth?
Detail_lesson: A test written from the implementation passes by construction. It describes what the code does, which is what you already had, rather than what the code should do, which is the only thing worth asserting. Everyone can see the problem. The disagreement is about the fix, and it is a real disagreement: keep the expectation human-authored and let the agent write only the scaffolding; have one agent write from the spec while another writes the implementation, without either seeing the other; attack the suite with mutations and treat any surviving mutant as a missing test; or accept the tests as regression-only and move real verification into staged rollout and production signal. Each of those costs something. Say which cost you would pay.
CustomInstruction: Pick one and name its cost. Every option here trades either speed or coverage for confidence.

Title: You get paged for a change no human read. What changes on Monday?
Detail_lesson: This is the part that arrives whether or not anyone planned for it. The volume of merged change goes up, the fraction any individual has read goes down, and eventually something breaks at 2am and the person holding the pager is meeting the code for the first time under load. There is a policy answer, a tooling answer, and a fatalist answer, and engineers who have carried a pager tend to disagree sharply about which one is honest. Do you cap agent autonomy at some blast-radius line and defend it; do you make rollback and isolation so cheap that understanding is genuinely optional; or do you accept that debugging is now itself an agent task and change what you expect of the on-call human? Answer from your own rotation.
CustomInstruction: Answer from a page you have actually taken. Say what you would change first, not everything you would change.

Title: What will you not hand over, and what does keeping it cost?
Detail_lesson: This one asks for a commitment rather than an observation. There is some part of the work you intend to keep doing yourself, and keeping it is not free: it costs throughput, it costs you the argument with whoever is measuring merged PRs, and if you are wrong it costs you a year. Naming the thing is easy. Naming its price is the part that makes the answer worth voting on. Common candidates: the interface decisions everything else hardens around, deciding what not to build, keeping production access human, and the one that gets least airtime, giving junior engineers the work that used to make them senior. Say what you keep and what you are paying for it.
CustomInstruction: State the thing and its price in the same answer. An answer with no cost in it is not a commitment.
